18	# PropGen: Automated Property Generation for Property-Based Testing of Mobile Apps
19	
20	- Authors: Xiong, Yiheng; Song, Shiwen; Ma, Bo; Su, Ting; Xie, Xiaofei
21	- Year / venue: 2026, Proceedings of the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (published)
22	- DOI: 10.1145/3832783.3837536 · URL: https://doi.org/10.1145/3832783.3837536
23	- Source text: `fulltext.txt` (page refs = PDF page index). The PDF is arXiv v2 (8 Oct 2026) carrying the ASE '26 camera-ready header and DOI (p. 1); peer-reviewed (received 2026-03-26, accepted 2026-06-18, p. 13).
24	
25	Labels: **[V]** verified in the paper's own data/tables/results · **[A]** author claim · **[I]** our interpretation.
26	Every [V]/[A] item ends with a page ref `(p. N)`. Write "not reported" when the paper does not say.
27	
28	## 1. Research objective
29	- [A] Automate the construction of properties for property-based testing (PBT) of mobile apps with LLMs. A *property* here is a rule of the form precondition -> interaction -> expected postcondition that must hold whenever it applies; PBT then generates many GUI event sequences and checks whether the rule is violated (p. 1, p. 3).
30	- [A] Motivation: non-crashing functional bugs lack explicit test oracles; PBT can expose them, but writing properties by hand is "difficult and expensive", and apps rarely have specifications (p. 1). Asking an LLM directly for properties is unreliable because, without evidence of how the app behaves, "LLMs tend to hallucinate properties that the app never satisfies" (p. 2).
31	
32	## 2. Research questions / hypotheses
33	- [V] RQ1: effectiveness in exploring app functionalities and generating valid properties; RQ2: how often properties are imprecise (cause false positives) and how well refinement fixes them; RQ3: whether generated properties find new functional bugs; RQ4: comparison with prior functional-testing techniques in finding new bugs (p. 6).
34	
35	## 3. Methodology
36	- Research design: [V] Tool design plus empirical evaluation on 12 Android apps, with human annotation of validity, comparison against baselines, and bug reporting to developers (p. 6-8).
37	- Approach / model / intervention: [V] PropGen has three stages (p. 3-6): (1) **hypothesis-guided exploration**: an MLLM looks at the screenshot (with numbered widgets from the accessibility tree), app name and activity names, and proposes candidate functionalities each tied to a triggering widget; PropGen executes them step by step, the MLLM labels each step success/fail/complete, and traces are summarised into "behavioral evidence" (state before, event, state after, state diff, outcome); random exploration is used when no unexplored hypothesis remains (p. 4-5); (2) **property synthesis**: the MLLM first writes a natural-language property (precondition P, interaction I, postcondition Q) from the evidence, then translates it into executable code for the PBT tool Kea (p. 6); (3) **feedback-driven refinement**: for properties whose reported violations are *manually confirmed* false positives, the LLM locates which of P, I or Q is imprecise using the source trace and the failing run, and edits only that part (p. 4, p. 6).
38	- Baselines or comparison conditions: [V] RQ1: DroidAgent (LLM-based functionality exploration) and a naive LLM baseline that writes 20 properties per app from the app's official description without running the app (p. 7). RQ4: Genie, Odin (automated differential oracles), PBFDroid (PBT for data-manipulation functionalities) and VisionDroid (LLM multi-agent functional bug detection) (p. 7).
39	
40	## 4. Dataset and sample
41	- Data source(s): [V] 12 popular open-source Android apps (e.g. OmniNotes, Markor, AnkiDroid, NewPipe), 57,529 to 403,785 LOC; GitHub stars 1.1K-37.5K (p. 7).
42	- Sample size (N) and unit: [V] 12 apps. Units of analysis: 1,282 functionalities inferred by PropGen (575 by DroidAgent), 985 generated properties, 240 naive-baseline properties, 127 imprecise properties, 25 new bugs (p. 8-10).
43	- Sampling / selection method: [V] Eight apps adopted from prior functional-bug studies, excluding apps no longer runnable/maintained or functionally similar to already chosen ones; four more popular open-source Google Play apps added "to further improve diversity" (p. 6-7). No power or sample-size reasoning reported.
44	- Data availability (public? link?): [A] "We have made all the artifacts publicly available" (p. 11), Zenodo artifact doi:10.5281/zenodo.21770804 (p. 13). Not checked by us.
45	
46	## 5. Experimental setup
47	- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] Ubuntu 22.04, 192 CPU cores (AMD EPYC 9654), official Android 11 Pixel emulators; GPT-5.2 (snapshot gpt-5.2-2025-12-11) as backend MLLM for PropGen and DroidAgent with default decoding (temperature 1.0, top-p 1.0); 3 h per app for evidence construction and property synthesis, then 6 h of Kea PBT per app (p. 7). Built on DroidBot, uiautomator2 and ADB; mainly Python and JavaScript (p. 6). RQ4 time budgets aligned: 9 h per app for Genie, Odin and VisionDroid; 6 h testing for PBFDroid after the authors manually wrote its DMF properties (p. 8). DroidAgent's time budget is not stated explicitly (not reported).
48	- Human annotation: [V] two graduate students in software engineering (each at least four years of Android experience), not co-authors, labelled independently; Cohen's kappa 0.91 (functionality validity), 0.82 (execution correctness), 0.81 (property validity); disagreements then resolved by discussion (p. 7).
49	- Code availability: [A] artifacts released on Zenodo (p. 11, p. 13).
50	
51	## 6. Evaluation metrics
52	- Metric — what it measures — why chosen:
53	  - [V] **Functionality validity**: share of inferred functionalities that really exist in the app (human judged from screenshot) (p. 7).
54	  - [V] **Execution correctness**: share of inferred functionalities whose executed event sequence actually realises them (human judged) (p. 7).
55	  - [V] **Property validity**: property is valid only if every referenced widget/event appears in its source trace (automated groundedness check) and annotators judge P, I and Q faithful to the intended functionality (p. 7). Chosen because "mobile apps lack ground-truth specifications" (p. 7). Validity does not imply precision (p. 7).
56	  - [V] **Refinement success**: revised property must (a) still hold on its source trace, (b) no longer raise the spurious violation, and (c) be confirmed valid and intent-preserving by humans (p. 8).
57	  - [V] **New bugs**: manually confirmed, previously unreported functional bugs, reported to developers (p. 8); for RQ4 also a manual **scope analysis** of whether each prior tool's oracle could in principle detect each bug, partly validated by consulting authors of Genie, Odin and PBFDroid (p. 8).
58	  - [V] **Cost**: tokens and USD per LLM call and per app (p. 9).
59	- Statistical testing (tests used, significance, effect sizes, confidence intervals): [V] None; counts and percentages from a single run per tool and app (p. 8-10). Only inter-rater agreement (Cohen's kappa) is reported (p. 7).
60	
61	## 7. Key findings
62	1. PropGen inferred 1,282 functionalities, 1,210 valid (94.4%) and 977 correctly executed (76.2%), vs DroidAgent 575 inferred, 491 valid (85.4%), 187 correctly executed (32.5%) — [V] (p. 8, p. 9).
63	2. PropGen generated 985 properties, 912 valid (92.6%; 78.7%-98.8% per app) — [V] (p. 8). The naive LLM baseline (app description only) produced 240 properties, none valid, because it referenced non-existent widgets — [V] (p. 9).
64	3. 127 properties caused false positives during PBT; 118 (92.9%) were successfully refined, mostly by changing the postcondition (64) or precondition (53), only 1 by changing the interaction; of 9 failures, 5 were misdiagnoses and 4 drifted from the original intent — [V] (p. 9).
65	4. Properties found 25 previously unknown functional bugs in the latest app versions; 5 fixed by developers at writing time; categories: functionality does not take effect (12), state inconsistency (6), unexpected wrong behaviour (4), navigation failure (3) — [V] (p. 9-10).
66	5. Of the 25 bugs, only 7 (28%) were in the detection scope of the four prior tools and 3 (12%) were rediscovered; the prior tools together found 13 unknown bugs, of which PropGen missed 10 — [V] (p. 10). [A] The approaches are "complementary rather than substitutable" (p. 10).
67	6. Cost: about $14.86 and 6,364k tokens per app for PropGen vs $13.01 and 5,109k tokens for DroidAgent; refinement about $0.02 per property — [V] (p. 9).
68	
69	## 8. Limitations stated by the authors
70	- [A] Manual inspection of functionalities and properties may introduce subjectivity and bias; mitigated by two independent annotators and consensus (p. 11).
71	- [A] The 12 apps may not represent the diversity of real-world apps; a larger and broader set is planned (p. 11).
72	- [A] Open-source apps may be in GPT-5.2's training data; mitigated by checking that none of the 25 bugs was previously reported, and by noting that six of the 12 tested builds were released after the model's training cutoff and still yielded bugs (p. 11).
73	- [A] Failure modes: the MLLM sometimes proposes non-existent functionalities, executions may not finish within the step budget or are labelled successful too early, and synthesis occasionally hallucinates widgets despite grounding (p. 9). PropGen generates only one property per functionality and lacks the differential oracles of Genie/Odin (p. 10).
74	- [A] A pre-existing app fault could in principle corrupt generated or refined properties; risk argued to be limited because properties come only from successful traces and refinements are human-confirmed (p. 10-11).
75	
76	## 9. Limitations we identified
77	- [I] **Not fully automatic.** Refinement is triggered only after a human confirms a violation is a false positive (p. 4, p. 6), and bug confirmation is manual (p. 8). The cost of this human effort is not reported.
78	- [I] **Single run with temperature 1.0.** Each tool runs once per app (p. 8) with stochastic decoding (p. 7); no variance or repeat runs are reported, so it is unknown how stable the counts are.
79	- [I] **Weak naive baseline.** The naive baseline sees only the app's description, never the GUI (p. 7). Its 0/240 result shows that runtime evidence is needed, but does not test simpler runtime-grounded alternatives.
80	- [I] **Possible author-tool bias.** Kea and PBFDroid come from overlapping author groups (refs [52], [71], p. 12-13), and the PBFDroid properties used in RQ4 were written by the authors (p. 8). The scope analysis is manual (p. 8). These choices could favour PropGen, though consulting the original tool authors partly mitigates this.
81	- [I] **Contamination check is partial.** "Not previously reported" bugs (p. 11) do not show that the model lacks prior knowledge of app behaviour; app functionality, not bugs, is what the model may have memorised.
82	- [I] **Validity is judged against human understanding, not a specification** (p. 7). This is reasonable but means "valid" depends on annotators' familiarisation of at least fifteen minutes per app (p. 7).
83	
84	## 10. Threats to validity
85	- Internal (confounds, leakage, selection): [I] Same MLLM backend for PropGen and DroidAgent (p. 7) is a fair control. Budget alignment across tools in RQ4 (p. 8) is reasonable, but tools differ in design scope, which the authors address with the scope analysis (p. 8). Possible training-data exposure of open-source apps (p. 11).
86	- External (generalisability of sample/context): [I] 12 open-source Android apps on emulators (p. 7); unclear transfer to iOS, web, closed-source or login/network-heavy apps.
87	- Construct (do metrics measure the concept?): [I] "Valid" properties are grounded and faithful but may still be imprecise (p. 7); bug counts depend on each tool's oracle type, which the authors acknowledge ("Raw bug counts alone are therefore not directly comparable", p. 8).
88	- Statistical conclusion (power, multiple comparisons, variance): [I] No statistical tests; 12 apps; single run (p. 8). High kappa values (0.81-0.91, p. 7) support annotation reliability.
89	- Reproducibility (data/code/setup reported?): [I] Good: model snapshot, decoding parameters, budgets, hardware and artifacts are reported (p. 7, p. 13). Proprietary model dependence and temperature 1.0 limit exact replication.
90	
91	## 11. Future research directions
92	- Stated by authors [A] (p. 9-11): evaluate on a larger and broader set of apps (p. 11); interact-then-infer functionality inference, activity transition graphs for step planning, explicit completion checks, post-synthesis widget checks (p. 9); richer context and an intent-verification step for refinement (p. 9); more properties per functionality and combining PropGen with specialised oracles (p. 10).
93	- Suggested by us [I]: use properties mined from an original app as a behavioural oracle for an AI-reconstructed version of that app (differential fidelity testing), and measure how many original-app properties the rebuild satisfies.
94	
95	## 12. Relevance to our research
96	- Research questions addressed (RQ ids): RQ2, RQ4, RQ5 (indirect); RQ1 only tangentially. Not RQ3.
97	- How it informs our work [I]: PropGen does not generate or reconstruct applications, so it gives no direct evidence on fidelity or code quality of AI-built apps. Its value is as a method: it recovers behavioural specifications from a running black-box app (no source, no spec), which is exactly the kind of oracle a reverse-engineering study needs to check functional fidelity (RQ2, RQ5). Its result that an LLM without runtime observation produces 0 valid properties (p. 9) supports grounding any reconstruction or test generation in observed behaviour. Its evaluation design (independent annotators with kappa, scope analysis for oracle-dependent tools) is a good template for RQ4. Relevance is therefore medium.
98	
99	## 13. Evidence table (for the evidence matrix)
100	| RQ | Claim | Page | Label | Strength |
101	|---|---|---|---|---|
102	| RQ2 | Behavioural properties can be recovered from a running Android app without specs: 912 of 985 LLM-generated properties judged valid (92.6%) | 8, 9 | V | moderate |
103	| RQ2 | An LLM given only the app description produced 240 properties, none valid (hallucinated widgets); runtime evidence is required | 9 | V | moderate |
104	| RQ2 | Generated properties found 25 previously unknown functional bugs in 12 apps; prior tools rediscovered only 3 | 9, 10 | V | moderate |
105	| RQ4 | Validity judged by 2 independent non-author annotators (kappa 0.91 / 0.82 / 0.81); no ground-truth spec exists for apps | 7 | V | moderate |
106	| RQ4 | Bug counts across functional-testing tools are oracle-dependent and not directly comparable; scope analysis used instead | 8, 10 | V | moderate |
107	| RQ4 | Single run per tool and app at temperature 1.0; no variance or statistical tests reported | 7, 8 | V | moderate |
108	| RQ5 | Imprecise LLM properties are common (127 of 985 caused false positives) but 92.9% could be refined, mainly via pre/postconditions | 9 | V | moderate |
109	
110	Strength note [I]: moderate = peer-reviewed (ASE 2026) single study with 12 apps and good annotation reliability, but no replication or variance.
111	
112	## 14. Key quotes
113	> "none of which is valid" (p. 9)
114	
115	> "Raw bug counts alone are therefore not directly comparable across" (p. 8)
116	
117	> "Neither annotator is a co-author" (p. 7)
118	
119	## Analyst notes
120	- Reading coverage: sections read / skipped and why: all 13 PDF pages read via `fulltext.txt` (abstract to conclusion, data availability, acknowledgements); reference list (p. 12-13) skimmed for author overlap only. Figures 1-2 (p. 3) are diagrams whose content is described in the text. The two-column layout interleaves lines in `fulltext.txt`; all numbers were taken from tables and checked against the text.
121	- Uncertainties: (1) DroidAgent's exploration time budget in RQ1 is not stated explicitly; (2) the human effort for confirming false positives and bugs is not quantified; (3) the abstract in metadata.json is truncated, but the full text was available; (4) the 25 bugs' report links/IDs on public trackers are not given in the paper (Table 4 lists IDs 1-25 internal to the paper, p. 10).
122	- Funding [V]: National Research Foundation Singapore / CyberSG R&D Programme Office and NSFC projects (p. 11); no conflict of interest statement beyond this.

405	4     E VALUATION AND M ETRICS
406	
407	4.1    E VALUATION P ROTOCOL
408	
409	The evaluation of generated code C is conducted using a deterministic executor built upon the
410	browser-use library (browser-use, 2025). This executor programmatically interacts with the ren-
411	
412	
413	                                                                6
414	
415	=== [PDF page 7] ===
416	
417	dered webpage by sequentially executing each pre-defined action ai from the ground-truth action
418	trajectory T . This design isolates the evaluation to code execution and removes any dependency on
419	high-level task planning, thereby ensuring a stable and reproducible protocol.
420	The evaluation of the trajectory proceeds step-by-step. At each step i, the action ai is attempted. The
421	action is considered a failure under two conditions: (1) it is operationally infeasible (e.g., a target
422	element is not found), or (2) its corresponding logical assertions li are not satisfied.
423	For logical assertion verification, an MLLM judge, specifically Gemini-2.5-Pro (Comanici et al.,
424	2025), is employed to analyze screenshots of the page state before and after an action to determine
425	its correctness. The prompt for this judge is detailed in Appendix E. Upon the successful completion
426	of an action, a new screenshot is captured. If the visual evaluation flag vi for this step is true, the new
427	screenshot undergoes a visual fidelity assessment. This assessment is based on a composite score
428	that integrates OCR-based text similarity (Cui et al., 2025), DINO-based structural similarity (Oquab
429	et al., 2023), and a high-level evaluation also conducted by Gemini-2.5-Pro (see Appendix E for
430	the prompt). Actions where vi is false, which typically involve insignificant or stochastic visual
431	changes, are omitted from this visual assessment phase.
432	
433	4.2   M ETRICS
434	
435	Model performance is quantified through a hierarchy of metrics designed to measure functional
436	correctness, visual fidelity, and overall task completion.
437	
438	Interactive Functionality Score (IFS). This metric measures a model’s ability to generate func-
439	tionally correct code. An action ai from the trajectory T is considered successful if and only if
440	it executes without operational errors and all associated logical assertions li are satisfied, as deter-
441	mined by the protocol in Section 4.1. The IFS is defined as the ratio of successfully completed
442	actions (Nsucc ) to the total number of actions (Ntotal ).
443	                                                         Nsucc
444	                                               IFS =                                                   (1)
445	                                                         Ntotal
446	
447	Visual Fidelity Score (VFS). The VFS assesses the visual quality of the rendered user interface.
448	This score is computed exclusively over checkpoints that were successfully reached and have the
449	visual evaluation flag enabled (vi = true). Let Iv,succ be the set of indices for these qualifying
450	checkpoints. The score for each checkpoint i ∈ Iv,succ is a weighted combination of two compo-
451	nents: a Low-level Visual Score (SLVS,i ), which averages an OCR-based Levenshtein similarity and a
452	DINO-based cosine similarity, and a High-level Visual Score (SHVS,i ), which is a holistic assessment
453	from the MLLM judge. The final VFS is the macro-average of these checkpoint scores. The weight
454	w is set to 0.5 based on validation studies (Section 5.4).
455	                                   1       X
456	                       VFS =                   (w · SLVS,i + (1 − w) · SHVS,i )                   (2)
457	                                |Iv,succ |
458	                                         i∈Iv,succ
459	
460	
461	Final Score. The Final Score is defined by combining the IFS and VFS with fixed weights. For
462	steps where actions cannot be executed, no images are available to compute visual similarity scores.
463	An alternative weighting scheme based on the ratio of successful (Nsucc ) to total (Ntotal ) steps was ex-
464	plored, but it proved ineffective for differentiating model performance. Therefore, a simple weighted
465	combination is adopted with the weighting factor α set to 0.7 (see Section 5.4). By assigning sub-
466	stantial weight to the IFS component, the impact of unreachable states on overall evaluation is ap-
467	propriately reflected. All reported scores are macro-averaged across the entire benchmark.
468	                                Final Score = α · IFS + (1 − α) · VFS                                  (3)

523	
524	This selection encompasses both proprietary and open-source models, as well as specialized video
525	understanding models. The full list of evaluated models and their performance is detailed in Table 3.
526	Implementation Details. For each task in IWR-Bench, models are provided with the user inter-
527	action video and a composite image of all crawled static assets. To accommodate models without
528	native video support, each video is sampled at 1 fps, with the number of frames capped at 64.
529	Videos exceeding 64 seconds are uniformly downsampled to meet this limit. The video (or its sam-
530	pled frames) and the composite image are arranged as a sequential, multi-image input. The task is to
531	generate a single, self-contained HTML file that integrates all necessary CSS and JavaScript to repli-
532	cate the observed webpage. All other inference parameters utilize the default settings recommended
533	by the model providers. The complete prompt templates are detailed in Appendix E.
534	
535	5.2   M AIN R ESULTS
536	
537	The comprehensive evaluation results on IWR-Bench are presented in Table 3. The findings reveal a
538	clear performance landscape, highlighting the substantial difficulty of the task and surfacing several
539	key observations regarding current model capabilities, with case studies provided in Appendix F.
540	A Clear Performance Hierarchy Is Observed Across Model Categories. The results on IWR-
541	Bench show a pronounced performance stratification across model categories. Proprietary multi-
542	modal large language models are positioned in the upper echelon, with GPT-5 obtaining the high-
543	est Final Score (36.35). This is followed by a competitive cluster that includes Claude-Sonnet-4
544	(thinking) (34.62), Claude-Opus-4 (thinking) (34.13), Doubao-seed-1.6 (34.02), and Claude-Sonnet-
545	4 (34.00). The top-performing open-source model, Qwen3-VL (thinking), has a score of 31.15. This
546	
547	
548	                                                        8
549	
550	=== [PDF page 9] ===
551	
552	score is lower than that of the leading proprietary group but surpasses several mid-tier proprietary
553	entries, such as GPT-4o (latest) (29.55). At the lower end of the performance spectrum, video-
554	specialized models like VideoLLaMA3-7B (13.67) and InternVideo-2.5-Chat-8B (10.07) are found.
555	This hierarchy indicates that general multimodal reasoning and code generation capabilities are more
556	critical for success on IWR-Bench than specialized video-processing architectures.
557	Interactive Functionality Remains the Primary Performance Bottleneck. A substantial perfor-
558	mance gap exists between static visual replication and dynamic functionality implementation. This
559	gap is reflected in the consistently higher Visual Fidelity Scores (VFS) compared to the Interactive
560	Functionality Scores (IFS). For instance, GPT-5 obtains the highest visual metrics (LVS 68.29, HVS
561	60.21, VFS 64.25), yet its corresponding IFS is only 24.39. A similar pattern is observed for Claude-
562	Sonnet-4, which has the second-highest VFS (61.34) but an IFS of only 22.29. The difficulty of this
563	task is further underscored by the low absolute IFS values, with the highest score remaining below
564	25, highlighting that interactive webpage reconstruction is a largely unsolved problem.
565	Reasoning Enhancement Provides Consistent but Moderate Gains. Consistent but moderate
566	performance improvements are observed when using reasoning-enhanced inference. For instance,
567	the ”thinking” variant of Claude-Sonnet-4 shows higher performance in both Final Score (34.62
568	vs. 34.00) and IFS (23.65 vs. 22.29). A similar trend is noted for Claude-Opus-4 (Final 34.13
569	vs. 33.33; IFS 23.61 vs. 21.83) and Gemini-2.5-Pro (Final 30.36 vs. 30.31; IFS 21.65 vs. 20.51).
570	This evidence indicates that while enhanced reasoning acts as a useful refinement, the base model’s
571	capability remains the primary factor determining the performance ceiling on IWR-Bench.
572	
573	5.3   P ERFORMANCE A NALYSIS ACROSS TASK D IMENSIONS
574	
575	A fine-grained analysis (detailed in Appendix B) reveals distinct performance patterns. The synthe-
576	sis of event-driven functionality is the primary bottleneck, evidenced by a sharp performance drop
577	from static (L1) to interactive (L2-L4) tasks (Table 4). Models also struggle with highly structured
578	layouts (Table 5). Performance varies by domain, with relative strength in ”Entertainment & Media”
579	(Table 6), pointing to structured code generation and state management as key research directions.
580	
581	5.4   VALIDATION OF THE E VALUATION P ROTOCOL
582	
583	The robustness and reliability of the evaluation protocol are validated through a rigorous, two-part
584	analysis that addresses both the metric parameters and the agent-as-a-judge methodology (Zheng
585	et al., 2023; Gou et al., 2025; Maaz et al., 2023). First, the weighting coefficients (w and α) for the
586	scoring metrics are determined through a human alignment study, with the detailed procedure and re-
587	sults presented in Appendix C. Second, the agent-as-a-judge framework is validated through a multi-
588	stage process. This process includes a meticulous cross-verification of annotated action trajectories
589	(Section 3.2), automated verification of logical assertions using an MLLM-based judge(Comanici
590	et al., 2025), and manual inspection of the agent’s operational fidelity. For the manual inspection,
591	three PhD students observed the agent’s execution on 100 randomly sampled, model-generated web-
592	pages, with the browser’s headless mode disabled to compare on-screen behavior against evaluation
593	logs. Failures in the agent’s evaluation were observed in only three instances. These issues typically
594	stemmed from ambiguous element descriptors (e.g., buttons with identical names), which required
595	a more precise locator (d i). All identified discrepancies were subsequently rectified.
596	
597	6     C ONCLUSION
598	This paper introduces IWR-Bench, the first benchmark designed to evaluate Interactive Webpage
599	Reconstruction from video. Through an automated agent-as-a-judge evaluation protocol, perfor-
600	mance is quantified using two metrics: the IFS and the VFS. Comprehensive evaluations on 28
601	LVLMs reveal a stark disparity between visual replication and functional implementation. While
602	models achieve moderate success in reconstructing static appearance (VFS), their ability to generate
603	correct, event-driven logic remains critically limited, as shown by low IFS scores across the board.
604	This finding indicates that the primary bottleneck for current models is not visual understanding but
605	the synthesis of complex interaction logic. IWR-Bench thus establishes a challenging new frontier
606	for vision-language research, highlighting the need for future work to focus on temporal reasoning,
607	dynamic asset binding, and robust code synthesis to create truly functional web applications.
608	
609

896	=== [PDF page 16] ===
897	
898	A    M ULTI -D IMENSIONAL TASK TAXONOMY
899	To move beyond a monolithic view of difficulty and enable a fine-grained analysis of model capabil-
900	ities, we developed a three-dimensional taxonomy to classify each task. This taxonomy categorizes
901	tasks along the orthogonal axes of Interaction Complexity, Visual Complexity, and Application Do-
902	main, providing a structured framework to understand the specific challenges inherent in each task
903	and to diagnose model failure modes with high precision.
904	
905	Interaction Complexity (L1-L4) This first axis categorizes tasks based on the depth of logical
906	and temporal understanding required for successful reconstruction.
907	      • L1: Static Content Consumption. Tasks involve passive information consumption, pri-
908	        marily requiring correct handling of vertical scrolling to reconstruct long pages that extend
909	        beyond a single viewport (e.g., browsing a blog post or a project’s README).
910	      • L2: Simple State Manipulation. Tasks feature components that manage local state, such
911	        as filtering e-commerce results, switching between on-page tabs, or expanding/collapsing
912	        accordion menus. This level tests the generation of basic client-side event handlers.
913	      • L3: Complex Workflow Interaction. These tasks involve multi-step, sequential inter-
914	        actions where state is passed between components, such as a multi-step product config-
915	        urator or an online booking process. This tests understanding of application logic and
916	        inter-component communication.
917	      • L4: Algorithmic/Game Logic. The most complex level requires the model to reverse-
918	        engineer and implement a set of rules or algorithms, such as an online calculator, a text-
919	        based puzzle, or a simple game like 2048.
920	
921	Visual Complexity (V1-V4) This second axis captures the static challenge of rendering the web-
922	page’s appearance, focusing on its layout and styling.
923	      • V1: Minimalist Layouts. Simple, single- or two-column structures with standard element
924	        alignment, typical of documentation or text-heavy sites.
925	      • V2: Standard Grid-based Layouts. Organized grid systems are used in e-commerce or
926	        news portals, featuring numerous but regularly arranged elements.
927	      • V3: Asymmetric & Modern Layouts. Visually-driven designs with complex CSS, such
928	        as overlapping elements, parallax scrolling, and non-standard component shapes.
929	      • V4: Data-Dense Layouts. Dashboards or admin panels with a high density of information
930	        presented in charts, tables, and data cards, testing the ability to generate precise, repetitive
931	        structures.
932	
933	Application Domain To ensure our benchmark reflects the breadth of real-world web applications,
934	the third axis classifies tasks by their Application Domain. Drawing inspiration from established
935	taxonomies in web-centric agent research (Gou et al., 2025), we group tasks into five high-level
936	domains: Commerce & Services (e-commerce, booking, finance), Knowledge & Education (aca-
937	demic sites, news portals, documentation), Productivity & Tools (calculators, project management
938	boards), Entertainment & Media (games, streaming platforms), and Lifestyle & Community (so-
939	cial forums, blogs). This classification guarantees that models are evaluated across a diverse spec-
940	trum of functionalities and visual paradigms. For instance, a task involving filtering products on an
941	e-commerce site is tagged as [L2, V2, Commerce], while a task requiring the reconstruction of a
942	simple browser game is tagged as [L4, V1, Entertainment]. This multi-dimensional labeling allows
943	us to analyze whether a model’s performance correlates with certain types of interactions, visual
944	styles, or application contexts.

999	The VFS and Final Score metrics rely on the weighting coefficients w and α. These parameters are
1000	determined and validated through a human alignment study. A sample of 60 evaluation instances
1001	is constructed by selecting outputs from three randomly chosen models for each of 20 randomly
1002	selected tasks from IWR-Bench. Each instance is assessed by five PhD-level students on two di-
1003	mensions: visual fidelity and overall quality. To determine the optimal parameters, a grid search
1004	is performed over the discrete set {0.1, 0.2, . . . , 0.9} for both w and α. The value that maximizes
1005	the Spearman’s ρ correlation between the automated scores and the aggregated human judgments is
1006	selected. For the VFS metric, the peak correlation (ρ = 0.57) is observed at w = 0.5, indicating an
1007	equal weighting between LVS and HVS. For the Final Score, the maximum correlation with human
1008	overall judgment (ρ = 0.65) is achieved with α = 0.7, empirically validating the decision to weigh
1009	functionality (IFS) more heavily than visual fidelity (VFS).
1010	
1011	D    TASK AND ACTION R EPRESENTATION
1012	
1013	Each task in IWR-Bench is formally defined by an ‘action sequence‘, a structured list of discrete
1014	actions that an automated agent must perform to validate the reconstructed webpage. This rep-
1015	resentation standardizes the evaluation process. We defined a vocabulary of atomic actions, in-
1016	cluding Click(description), Type(key, description), Scroll(direction, amount, description), and
1017	Press(key, description). A crucial design choice is the use of a natural language ‘description‘ field
1018	for targeting elements instead of unstable positional coordinates (e.g., ”Click the primary ’Submit’
1019	button” instead of ”Click at (x:120, y:350)”). This makes the evaluation robust to minor layout vari-
1020	ations in the generated code and tests a more semantic understanding of the page structure, both for
1021	the model during generation and the agent during evaluation.

1138	Case 1 Analysis: E-commerce Workflow Simulation. Our first case study, classified as [L2, V2,
1139	E-commerce], simulates a fundamental e-commerce user journey to test a model’s ability to handle
1140	sequential state manipulations within a standard visual structure. The task requires the model to
1141	replicate a workflow involving filtering a product grid by a specific brand, sorting the filtered results
1142	by price and adding a selected item to the shopping cart.
1143	As illustrated in Figure 8, this task effectively exposes different failure modes in different models.
1144	On the left, Claude-Sonnet-4 demonstrates good capabilities in static replication and simple state
1145	management. It accurately renders the initial layout and correctly implements the action for filtering
1146	and sorting. However, its failure occurs at the final ”add to cart” step. The right side shows the result
1147	of GPT-5. This case likely involved too many static resources, causing the product list on the initial
1148	page to fail to render successfully. By pinpointing these different stages of failure, the benchmark
1149	provides a granular diagnosis of each model’s specific strengths and weaknesses in front-end code
1150	generation.

1157	the input video. The visual complexity is simple (V2), deliberately shifting the evaluation focus from
1158	layout replication to the correctness of the underlying algorithmic logic. The The core challenge is
1159	to deduce and codify the game’s state-transition functions, including tile movement, merging logic,
1160	and the spawning of new tiles.

    on functionality-level evaluation beyond structural coverage met-
    rics [7, 75]. The manual evaluation is conducted by two graduate
    students in software engineering, each with at least four years of
    Android development experience. Neither annotator is a co-author
    or was involved in developing PropGen, which reduces assessment

    bias. Before the annotation, each annotator was given at least fif-


    teen minutes to familiarize themselves with the functionalities of
    every subject app. During this process, annotators also referred
    to the app’s official introduction page when available, so that the
    subsequent judgments were made with sufficient understanding

    of the app’s functionalities. In addition, annotators could interact


    with the running app at any time to verify uncertain cases.
        For each inferred functionality, we evaluate two aspects. The
    first is functionality validity, which examines whether the inferred
    functionality actually exists in the app. Annotators are given the
    inferred functionality description together with the GUI screenshot
    from which it was inferred, and determine whether the described
    functionality is genuinely supported by the interface. The second
    is execution correctness, which examines whether the system cor-
    rectly executes the inferred functionality. For each inferred func-
    tionality, annotators are provided with the corresponding execution
    screenshots and interaction events, and judge whether the executed
    interaction sequence indeed realizes the intended functionality.
        Because mobile apps lack ground-truth specifications, we cannot
    decide a property’s validity against a reference oracle. We therefore
    assess validity along two complementary layers, one checked by an
    automated proxy and the other by human annotators. The ground-
    edness layer is verified by an automated proxy: we automatically
    check that every widget and event referenced in the property is
    observable in its source trace, so that the property is executable on
    the app rather than referring to hallucinated UI elements. The faith-
    fulness layer is judged by human annotators, who assess the three
    components: (1) whether the precondition appropriately constrains
    the UI state in which the property should be applied, (2) whether
    the interaction scenario accurately reflects the user interactions
    required to perform the functionality, and (3) whether the postcon-
    dition correctly captures the observable UI behavior that should

   and only 3 (12%) are actually found in practice. Genie, Odin, and


   PBFDroid rely on predefined automated oracles or manually speci-
   fied DMF properties, and can therefore only find the bug categories
   emphasized in their original designs, whereas PropGen targets

   more broadly. VisionDroid, in contrast, is a more general LLM-
   based approach, but its exploration validates a functionality by
   following one plausible interaction path at a time, whereas most
   bugs uncovered by PropGen are exposed only when a property is
   checked under specific event sequences.
      We further compare the overall bug-finding results. On the same
   12 apps, the four prior techniques together uncover 13 previously

   unknown functional bugs (Genie 3, Odin 3, PBFDroid 6, and Vi-

   sionDroid 4; the per-tool counts sum to 16 because three bugs are

   found by more than one tool), fewer than the 25 bugs uncovered

   by PropGen. Both counts follow the same criterion, i.e., every bug
   is manually confirmed to be a real, previously unknown functional
   bug; as reported in RQ3, 5 of those found by PropGen have already
   been fixed by developers. The 3 rediscovered bugs above are exactly
   the overlap between the two bug sets: PropGen finds 22 bugs that
   the prior techniques miss, while they find 10 that PropGen misses.
   The two are thus complementary rather than substitutable, as both
   directions stem from the oracles each side can check. PropGen
   misses those 10 bugs mainly because its generated properties do
   not cover the oracles these techniques rely on, e.g., the differential
   oracles of Genie and Odin; it also generates only one property per
   functionality, and generating more would cover more expected
   behaviors.
      The two bug sets also differ in type. The bugs found by each
   prior technique are concentrated in the category its oracle targets:
   all bugs found by PBFDroid are data manipulation errors; Genie
   and Odin mainly expose unexpected wrong behaviors; and Vision-
   Droid mainly exposes display errors. In contrast, the bugs found
   by PropGen span four categories reported in RQ3. PropGen there-
   fore achieves broader coverage without manual effort, but does not
   subsume a specialized oracle within its own niche; combining the
   two is a promising direction for future work.

## 9. Limitations we identified
- [I] **IFS and VFS are not comparable in scale.** VFS averages only over checkpoints that were "successfully reached" (p. 7). chen2025iwr/analysis.md:38:- Approach / model / intervention: [V] Each model receives the interaction video (sampled at 1 fps, max 64 frames) and a composite image of all crawled static assets, and must output one self-contained `index.html` with all HTML, CSS and JS; backend logic must be mocked in JS; no external libraries or fonts (p. 8, p. 20). Asset filenames are anonymised (e.g. `asset_001.png`) so models must match assets visually rather than by name (p. 5).
chen2025iwr/analysis.md:44:- Sampling / selection method: [V] 200 candidate tasks proposed by web-development experts -> deduplication and diversity balancing across domain, visual complexity and interaction logic -> 161 -> cross-verification by a second annotator and an LLM check of assertions -> disputed, ambiguous or overly trivial tasks removed -> 113 (p. 5-6). Exact criteria for "trivial" or "disputed" are not reported.
chen2025iwr/analysis.md:48:- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] Video sampled at 1 fps, capped at 64 frames (longer videos uniformly downsampled); video frames and asset image given as a sequential multi-image input; "All other inference parameters utilize the default settings recommended by the model providers" (p. 8). A standard system prompt is used for all models (p. 18, p. 20). Evaluation executor built on the `browser-use` library; Gemini-2.5-Pro is the MLLM judge for logical assertions and for the high-level visual score (p. 6-7). Actions target elements by natural-language description rather than coordinates (p. 17). Number of runs per model, temperature/seed and variance: not reported.
chen2025iwr/analysis.md:57:  - [V] Weights w = 0.5 and alpha = 0.7 were chosen by grid search to maximise Spearman's rho with human judgements of 60 instances (20 random tasks x 3 random models) rated by five PhD-level students; best rho = 0.57 for VFS and 0.65 for the Final Score (p. 17). Agreement among the five raters is not reported; their judgements were aggregated (p. 17).
xiong2026propgen/analysis.md:37:- Approach / model / intervention: [V] PropGen has three stages (p. 3-6): (1) **hypothesis-guided exploration**: an MLLM looks at the screenshot (with numbered widgets from the accessibility tree), app name and the activity names extracted from the AndroidManifest.xml file (p. 4), and proposes candidate functionalities each tied to a triggering widget; PropGen executes them step by step, the MLLM labels each step success/fail/complete, and traces are summarised into "behavioral evidence" (state before, event, state after, state diff, outcome); random exploration is used when no unexplored hypothesis remains (p. 4-5); widget signatures keep only app-defined text, filtered against "a whitelist extracted via static analysis" (p. 5); (2) **property synthesis**: the MLLM first writes a natural-language property (precondition P, interaction I, postcondition Q) from the evidence, then translates it into executable code for the PBT tool Kea (p. 6); (3) **feedback-driven refinement**: for properties whose reported violations are *manually confirmed* false positives, the LLM locates which of P, I or Q is imprecise using the source trace and the failing run, and edits only that part (p. 4, p. 6).
xiong2026propgen/analysis.md:43:- Sampling / selection method: [V] Eight apps adopted from prior functional-bug studies, excluding apps no longer runnable/maintained or functionally similar to already chosen ones; four more popular open-source Google Play apps added "to further improve diversity" (p. 6-7). No power or sample-size reasoning reported.
xiong2026propgen/analysis.md:47:- Procedure, settings, hyper-parameters, tools: [V] Ubuntu 22.04, 192 CPU cores (AMD EPYC 9654), official Android 11 Pixel emulators; GPT-5.2 (snapshot gpt-5.2-2025-12-11) as backend MLLM for PropGen and DroidAgent with default decoding (temperature 1.0, top-p 1.0); 3 h per app for evidence construction and property synthesis, then 6 h of Kea PBT per app (p. 7). Built on DroidBot, uiautomator2 and ADB; mainly Python and JavaScript (p. 6). RQ4 time budgets aligned: 9 h per app for Genie, Odin and VisionDroid; 6 h testing for PBFDroid after the authors manually wrote its DMF properties (p. 8). DroidAgent's time budget is not stated explicitly (not reported).
xiong2026propgen/analysis.md:56:  - [V] **Refinement success**: revised property must (a) still hold on its source trace, (b) no longer raise the spurious violation, and (c) be confirmed valid and intent-preserving by humans (p. 8).
xiong2026propgen/analysis.md:63:2. PropGen generated 985 properties, 912 valid (92.6%; 78.7%-98.8% per app) — [V] (p. 8). The naive LLM baseline (app description only) produced 240 properties, none valid, because it referenced non-existent widgets — [V] (p. 9).
